title: A healthy-food price wedge can exist without a detectable maternal or newborn health improvement
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35662, difference-in-differences and event-study evaluation of the Navajo Nation Healthy Diné Nation Act
geography: Navajo Nation; Healthy Diné Nation Act implemented in 2014-2015, with maternal and newborn outcomes from birth-certificate data

observations.period: 2014-2015 Healthy Diné Nation Act implementation and later birth-certificate outcome windows in the study

denominator.unit: Mothers and newborns recorded in the study's birth-certificate data; exact public abstract denominator not disclosed

policy_design.value: healthy foods and beverages were exempted from sales tax while unhealthy foods and beverages faced a tax increase, creating a 7% to 8% price wedge

maternal_newborn_health.value: no evidence that the policy improved the studied diet- and weight-related outcomes for mothers or newborns

gestational_diabetes_precision.value: estimates are precise enough to rule out improvements as large as those reported for U.S. city sugary-drink taxes

implementation_mechanisms.value: possible explanations include incomplete retailer implementation and cross-border shopping
implementation_mechanisms.unit: reported interpretation, not directly isolated mechanism estimate

purchases_and_cultural_response.value: not observed in the public abstract
purchases_and_cultural_response.unit: missing store-level price pass-through, purchases, cross-border trips, household budget, acceptability, and trust outcomes

observations.method: Difference-in-differences models and event studies using birth-certificate measures of maternal and newborn diet- and weight-related health conditions; the public abstract does not disclose the full comparison geography, sample counts, or implementation audit.
observations.uncertainty: A null health result does not show that the price wedge was absent or that no household changed purchases. The abstract leaves retailer compliance, cross-border shopping, product availability, exposure, and intermediate consumption pathways incompletely observed.
observations.subgroup: Mothers and newborns in the Navajo Nation outcome data; individual household shopping, retailer, community, and border-crossing patterns are not linked in the public abstract.
observations.counterinterpretation: The policy may have affected prices, purchases, revenue, or other outcomes not captured by the measured maternal/newborn endpoints. A place-specific null may reflect implementation and market geography rather than a universal failure of fiscal nutrition policy.

related_sources.claim: A separate 2026 NBER study finds short-run purchase and stigma effects from SNAP sugary-drink restrictions, providing a contrasting policy and outcome surface.

boundary: This record measures a place-specific fiscal food-policy design and a reported null result for maternal and newborn diet- and weight-related outcomes. It does not establish no change in purchases, no community benefit, cultural rejection, policy failure everywhere, or long-run health and household effects.
